notes: The earlier short circuit came from my own modelling. The catalogue's relay-module entry has no ports, so I attached every wire to relay1 with a null port. That merged 3V3, GND, D4 and the mains side into one node. I now name the relay's pins on each edge: VCC, GND and SIG on the low-voltage Grove side, and COM and NO on the switched mains side. The catalogue entry lists no ports, so these names are my own labels for the Grove relay's pins.

The relay is a switch, so the mains path is acc1 live -> relay COM, then relay NO -> socket terminal 1. Control and mains sides are separate nodes. The manual only says the relay interrupts the current path; it doesn't name relay terminals.

The relay's three low-voltage connections are modelled as three jumper wires: 3V3 -> VCC, GND -> GND, D4 -> SIG. The photo shows them going to the Grove connector. The manual doesn't say which relay pin each uses.

AC cable neutral goes directly to socket terminal 2 (twist or wire nut in the photo). The bulb screws into the socket on terminals 1 and 2. The bulb has a through path 1-2. The socket entry marks 1=2 only as interchangeable, not shorted, so I kept the bulb and socket joins.

Nano Matter pin layout and breadboard placement are assumed: the board straddles the centre channel in columns 1-15, left pins in row e and right pins in row f. The manual doesn't give columns. The jumper wires share strips with 3V3 (col 2), GND (col 14) and D4 (col 9).

The Google Nest Hub Max connects over Thread/Matter wirelessly, so it has no physical edges. The USB-C cable powers the Nano Matter and attaches with a null port because the catalogue's usb-cable has no ports.
The relay module is shown resting on the breadboard in the photo, so it has a contact edge with the breadboard.

notes: The relay-module catalogue entry has no ports, so wires and mains cables attach to relay1 with null ports. The three jumper wires carry 3V3 to VCC, GND to GND and D4 to the signal pin. The photo shows them going to the Grove connector. The manual doesn't say which relay pin each one uses.

The relay's switched contacts are modelled as: AC cable live -> relay -> lightbulb socket terminal 1. The AC cable neutral goes straight to socket terminal 2, joined with a twist or wire nut as in the photo. The manual only says the relay interrupts the current path.

Nano Matter pin layout and breadboard placement are assumed: the board straddles the centre channel in columns 1-15, left pins in row e and right pins in row f. The manual doesn't give the exact columns. Jumper wires are placed in the same column strips as the 3V3 (col 2), GND (col 14) and D4 (col 9) pins.

The Google Nest Hub Max connects over Thread/Matter wirelessly, so it is included as a part but has no physical edges. The USB-C cable powers the Nano Matter, with no port specified on the catalogue's usb-cable.
The relay module is shown resting on the breadboard in the photo, so it has a contact edge with the breadboard. The Matter and Google Home software steps have no hardware edges.

breadboard.port_rule: Holes are named '<column><bank>.<row>': column 1-30, bank 't' (top half, rows a-e) or 'b' (bottom half, rows f-j), e.g. '12t.c', '7b.h'. The 5 holes of one column-bank are one strip. Power rails: 'tp.<n>', 'tn.<n>', 'bp.<n>', 'bn.<n>' (each rail is one strip).
